name: Pomegranate
short: Case reports: allergy incl. exercise-induced anaphylaxis; possible warfarin interaction (INR changes) with juice. Reviews: may alter drug levels (e.g. tacrolimus). Trials: mostly mild-moderate events.
text: A 2024 systematic review of 66 clinical articles found side effects reported in 11, most commonly gastrointestinal problems, flu-like symptoms and urinary problems; 21 recorded no side effects and 34 did not mention them, and among 7 case reports the most significant reported side effect was allergic reaction. Case reports are titled as describing pomegranate-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis and pomegranate seed allergy in a child with multiple tree nut allergies. For warfarin, two case reports describe possible interactions: a 64-year-old woman whose INR (a blood-clotting measure) had been stable while she drank pomegranate juice 2 to 3 times a week had INRs below the target range after she stopped the juice, rated as a possible relationship, and a second case report of a potential interaction, which the authors said does not definitively prove an association between pomegranate juice and increased warfarin activity. A 2023 review states that pomegranate constituents inhibit the drug-metabolising enzymes CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, that observational studies reported pomegranate juice prolonged the effects of warfarin and sildenafil, that in preclinical studies prolonged intake of the juice increased the absorption of several drugs, and that clinical studies have so far used only single doses of juice; a review of tacrolimus interactions lists pomegranate juice among herbs that increased tacrolimus levels in human and/or animal models, without saying which applied to pomegranate. In contrast, in a single-dose crossover study in 14 healthy volunteers, pomegranate juice did not significantly affect blood levels of cyclosporine, with no difference in adverse events, and a 2015 review found no safety concern at the doses used in clinical studies but cautioned that pomegranate preparations may be harmful by inducing drug metabolism through activation of liver enzymes. In a placebo-controlled trial in 183 men with rising PSA after prostate cancer treatment, randomised to pomegranate extract, pomegranate juice or placebo, the majority of adverse events in the trial were of mild or moderate grade; the abstract does not say how adverse events were distributed between the groups or describe any more severe events; a pilot trial of a pomegranate extract in 64 overweight adults reported no serious adverse events.
